title: Emollients | NHS inform
text:
Emollients
Emollients are a type of moisturising treatment used to help certain skin conditions.
How emollients work
Emollients work by forming a protective layer on the skin which traps moisture and prevents water loss. This helps to soothe dry patches of skin and reduce itching. Emollients also help the skin repair itself, making the skin smoother and more hydrated.
Emollients are often used to help manage skin conditions that cause dry, itchy or scaly skin like
eczema
or
psoriasis
. They help prevent inflammation and flare-ups of these conditions.
Types of emollients
There are different types of emollients. These include:
Lotions
Emollient lotions are most commonly used to treat hairy or damaged areas of skin. For example, weeping eczema where pus is leaking out of damaged or broken skin. Lotions are thin and spread easily across the affected areas, but they’re not very moisturising.
Sprays
Sprays are absorbed quickly and used to treat areas that are hard to reach and painful. They are also used to treat infected skin that shouldn’t be touched.
Creams
Emollient creams are easy to apply and can be used during the day. They are not greasy and are absorbed quickly.
Ointments
Ointments are used to treat very dry, thickened skin. They should be used at night time as they can be very greasy and thick. Ointments are suitable for sensitive skin but should not be used on areas of broken skin.
Leave-on products
There are different types of leave-on products that can be applied directly to the skin.
Some leave-on products contain added ingredients that can help reduce
itching
or prevent infection. Many leave-on emollients can also be used to wash with.
Soap substitutes
Many soap, shampoo and shower gel products can dry out the skin, making skin conditions like
eczema
worse.
Leave-on products can be used as a soap substitute if you have dry or itchy skin.
You can get emollient soap substitutes that are used instead of normal soap in the bath or shower at your
local pharmacy
.
Your GP or local pharmacist will discuss which types of emollient will work best for your skin.
You may have try a few different emollients to find which one works best for you.
How to use emollients
Emollients should be applied directly to the skin. They can be used to replace lost moisture whenever your skin feels tight or dry.
You should apply them smoothly and avoid rubbing them into your skin. It helps to apply emollients in the same direction that your hair grows. This will help prevent hair follicles from getting blocked.
Emollients are very safe to use and you can’t overuse them.
You may need to try a combination of emollients before deciding which ones work best for you. For example, you may use a cream during the day and an ointment at night.
How to wash with emollients
Mix a small amount of leave-on product or soap substitute in the palm of your hand with some hot water and apply to damp or dry skin.
Rinse off the product or soap substitute and pat the skin dry, being careful not to rub it.
Leave-on products or substitutes do not foam like normal soap but work in the same way.
Speak to your local pharmacist if your skin stings and doesn’t settle after using an emollient wash product.
When to apply emollients
Emollients can be used as often as you need them to keep your skin moisturised and in good condition.
It’s important to apply emollients to parts of your body that are regularly exposed to the elements like your hands and face.
Emollients should be applied after washing your hands or body because this is when the skin needs more moisture. The emollient should be applied as soon as you’ve patted your skin dry to make sure it’s absorbed properly.
Using emollients with other skin treatments
If you’re using steroid creams or other treatments for your skin condition, you should wait 20 to 30 minutes between using the emollient and your other treatment. Your GP or healthcare professional will be able to advise you which one to use first.
Possible side effects
Emollients can sometimes cause a skin reaction. Symptoms of a skin reaction include:
a warm burning sensation or stinging that doesn’t settle after a few days
blocked or inflamed hair follicles (folliculitis) that may cause boils
rashes on the face that can irritate
acne
Speak to your GP, nurse or pharmacist if:
you have experienced a skin reaction to your emollient
you’re worried about your symptoms
Warnings and precautions
You should stay away from fire, flames and cigarettes when using emollients. Dressings, clothing and bedding that have been in contact with emollients can catch fire more easily. You should wash fabrics at a high temperature to prevent a build up of emollient.
